note: Single-pass extraction by Claude reading the paper text; evidence references sections/figures/tables. No multi-run validation.

components.description: DG-PRM: from fixed-criteria limitation to reward tree, allocation, Pareto optimization and results

nodes.name: Heuristic PRMs generalize poorly
nodes.description: Heuristic process rewards require objective, reference-based answers, often generalize poorly and are susceptible to reward hacking; generative process rewards still rely on a fixed set of standards that limits cross-domain adaptability.

nodes.name: Uniform negative rewards waste feedback
nodes.description: Prevailing approaches assign a uniform negative reward to incorrect steps, ignoring rich LLM-judgment details such as error severity and mistake type.

nodes.name: Reward tree of criteria
nodes.description: DG-PRM extracts reward criteria with a judge function over positive/negative output pairs, filters them with an automated validator, embeds them (BAAI/bge-en-icl, d=4096), and organizes them by incremental hierarchical clustering (BIRCH) into a tree of coarse parent and fine child criteria, merging criteria with cosine distance below xi=0.25.

nodes.name: Dynamic reward allocation
nodes.description: For each step, DG-PRM selects relevant parent criteria from the tree using a window of the previous mu=20 steps, generates fine-grained evaluation aspects, and matches child criteria whose cosine distance to an aspect is at most zeta=0.2, scoring each selected criterion.

nodes.name: Pareto-based preference pairs
nodes.description: DG-PRM computes the Pareto-optimal set over candidate steps given multi-criteria scores and forms preference pairs where Pareto-optimal steps dominate dominated ones, optimized with a step-wise DPO-style loss.

nodes.name: Reward quantity per step
nodes.description: DG-PRM selects about 3.7 reward criteria per step on average (1.5 coarse and 2.3 fine); QASC needs only coarse-grained criteria while specialized ChemistryQA needs more fine-grained ones.

nodes.name: Pareto filtering ablation
nodes.description: Pareto-based filtering improves accuracy over randomly pairing the highest-scoring sample, by 1.79% to 4.02% (e.g. ARC-c 90.63% to 94.65%), and over half of sampled steps are used for pair construction.

nodes.name: PRMBench state of the art
nodes.description: On PRMBench, DG-PRM improves R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on PS tasks from 45.6% to 62.4%, and improves DeepSeek-R1 overall from 69.5% to 76.5%, a new state of the art with a sensitivity average above 80%; generative models beat discriminative PRMs.

nodes.name: Gains on general, science, commonsense
nodes.description: DG-PRM boosts win rates on MT-Bench and Arena-Hard near human annotation, and on QASC, StrategyQA, ChemistryQA and ARC-c improves models at all sizes (1.5B-32B), even surpassing human annotation on StrategyQA; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B beats human performance on QASC and StrategyQA.

nodes.name: Better OOD generalization
nodes.description: In out-of-distribution settings ORM and Critic Direct drop sharply (sometimes below baseline) and Critic CoT drops on ChemistryQA, while DG-PRM generalizes well by selecting relevant rewards.

nodes.name: Training efficiency
nodes.description: DG-PRM matches Critic CoT accuracy with only 30% of the training steps, attributed to Pareto selection of representative positive and negative samples.

nodes.name: Lower cost than self-consistency
nodes.description: Compared with Critic CoT-SC(50), DG-PRM needs about half the compute while achieving 4.8% higher overall PRMBench performance; reward-tree construction costs about 7,000 input and 3,000 output tokens per sample, far below manual annotation, and the tree is reusable.

isolated_nodes.name: Defn: process reward model
isolated_nodes.description: A Process Reward Model assigns a reward to each intermediate step of a model output, providing dense supervision, unlike an outcome reward model which rewards only the final result.

isolated_nodes.name: Limitation: LLM-built criteria need human oversight
isolated_nodes.description: Reward criteria are constructed by LLMs and may not align with human expectations despite the validator, so human supervision is needed.

structural_reasoning: Argument runs from limitations of existing PRMs, through reward tree, allocation and Pareto optimization design, to benchmark, generalization, efficiency and cost evidence.
